questions.question: An engineer is designing two electromagnets, A and B. Both use the same type of wire and are connected to identical 6V power supplies. Electromagnet A has 100 turns of wire wrapped over 5 cm, while electromagnet B has 200 turns of wire wrapped over the same length. Assuming current is kept constant, why is electromagnet B stronger than A?
options: The increased number of turns increases the resistance, creating more heat which strengthens the magnetic field.
Having more turns of wire increases the total magnetic field generated because the magnetic fields from each turn add together.
Electromagnet B has a greater surface area of copper which attracts magnetic materials directly.
The extra turns of wire increase the voltage across the coil, making the magnet stronger.

questions.question: A student sets up an electromagnet and measures its strength. She increases the voltage of the power supply, which increases the current flowing through the coil. What happens to the magnetic field, and why?
options: The magnetic field becomes stronger because a larger current produces a stronger magnetic field around the wire.
The magnetic field becomes weaker because the increased current causes the wire to heat up, destroying the magnetism.
The magnetic field strength remains unchanged because field strength depends only on the number of turns in the coil.
The magnetic field becomes stronger because the current changes direction more rapidly at higher voltages.

questions.question: Two electromagnets, X and Y, have the same length of wire, number of turns, and current. On electromagnet X, the turns are wound very tightly together over 2 cm. On electromagnet Y, the turns are spaced out over 10 cm. Which statement correctly compares their magnetic fields?
options: Electromagnet Y is stronger because the field is spread over a larger physical area.
Electromagnet X is stronger because the closely spaced coils concentrate the magnetic field lines.
They have the same strength because they have the exact same number of turns and current.
Electromagnet Y is stronger because the spaced-out coils reduce magnetic interference between adjacent turns.

questions.question: A student tries to build an electromagnet by wrapping bare copper wire around a steel nail. The turns of wire are wrapped tightly and touch each other. When she connects the ends to a battery, the nail does not become magnetised. Why did this electromagnet fail to work?
options: Copper is a non-magnetic metal, so it can never be used to make an electromagnet.
The current flows straight across the touching bare turns along the nail rather than circulating around it in a coil.
Bare wire cannot conduct electricity unless it is insulated with plastic or enamel.
The touching bare wires create an air gap that blocks the magnetic field from entering the steel nail.

questions.question: Why is a soft iron core used to increase the strength of an electromagnet, rather than a core made of a non-magnetic material like wood?
options: Soft iron is an electrical insulator, which prevents current from leaking out of the wire coil.
Soft iron becomes magnetised when the electromagnet is turned on, adding its own magnetic field to the coil's field.
Soft iron physically squeezes the wire coil, forcing the electrical current to flow faster.
Soft iron generates its own permanent magnetic field that never turns off, keeping the electromagnet strong.

questions.question: When there is an electric current flowing through a straight copper wire, what is the effect on the space immediately surrounding the wire?
options: A magnetic field is created that forms concentric circles around the wire.
A static electric charge builds up in the air, creating a spark.
The wire becomes a permanent magnet with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.
No magnetic field is produced because copper is not a magnetic material.

questions.question: When a wire is wound into a coil (solenoid) and a current is passed through it, the magnetic field is much stronger than that of a single straight wire. What is the reason for this?
options: The coil shape increases the electrical resistance, which amplifies the magnetic force.
The magnetic field around each individual loop of wire adds together to produce a stronger combined field.
Coiling the wire converts the electrical current from direct current (DC) to alternating current (AC).
Coiling the wire causes the electrons to spin faster, which multiplies their individual magnetic charges.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a key operational feature of an electromagnet compared to a permanent magnet?
options: An electromagnet only has one pole, whereas a permanent magnet always has two.
An electromagnet can be turned on and off by controlling the electric current, whereas a permanent magnet's field is always active.
An electromagnet attracts only non-metals, while a permanent magnet attracts only metals.
An electromagnet works without any electrical energy once it has been initialised.

questions.question: If you break a permanent bar magnet carefully into two equal pieces, what is the result?
options: One piece becomes a pure north pole and the other becomes a pure south pole.
Two smaller magnets, each having both a north-seeking pole and a south-seeking pole.
Two pieces of ordinary, non-magnetic metal that no longer attract iron.
One piece that has two north poles and another piece that has two south poles.

questions.question: Two bar magnets are placed near each other. Magnet A has its north-seeking pole facing the north-seeking pole of Magnet B. What motion will be observed?
options: They will accelerate towards each other and stick together.
They will repel and move away from each other because similar magnetic poles repel.
They will remain completely still because only unlike poles can exert forces on each other.
They will demagnetise each other instantly without moving.

questions.question: A student has an unmarked metal bar. She wants to determine if it is a permanent magnet or just a magnetic material (like iron). She brings the north-seeking pole of a known bar magnet close to one end of the unmarked bar, and it is attracted. She then reverses the known magnet so the south-seeking pole is close to the same end of the unmarked bar. What result would prove that the unmarked bar is NOT a permanent magnet?
options: The bar is repelled by the south-seeking pole.
The bar is also attracted by the south-seeking pole.
The bar is unaffected by the south-seeking pole.
The bar starts to heat up rapidly.

questions.question: A recycling plant uses a magnetic separator to extract magnetic metals from a mixture of shredded waste. Which group of metals consists entirely of elements that will be attracted to the magnet?
options: Iron, cobalt, and nickel
Iron, copper, and aluminium
Cobalt, nickel, and zinc
Gold, silver, and copper

questions.question: A student suspends a bar magnet horizontally from a thread so it can rotate freely. After it stops moving, the north-seeking pole points towards the Earth's geographic North Pole. Why does this happen?
options: The geographic North Pole contains a massive deposit of copper which attracts the north-seeking pole.
The Earth has its own magnetic field, which aligns the suspended magnet's north-seeking pole.
The rotation of the Earth creates a mechanical force that pushes the north-seeking pole northward.
Gravity acts more strongly on the north-seeking pole of a magnet, pulling it downwards and northwards.

questions.question: A plotting compass is placed at various positions around a bar magnet. What determines the direction in which the compass needle points?
options: The needle always points directly towards the nearest geographic pole of the Earth, ignoring the bar magnet.
The needle lines up with the magnetic field of the bar magnet at that specific location.
The needle always points directly at the physical midpoint of the bar magnet.
The needle points perpendicular to the magnetic field lines due to electrostatic repulsion.

questions.question: A student is tracing a magnetic field line outside a bar magnet. If she follows the field line from its origin to its end, which path does it take?
options: From the south-seeking pole to the north-seeking pole.
From the north-seeking pole to the south-seeking pole.
From the center of the magnet outward to infinity in a straight line.
From the north-seeking pole, looping around to return to the same north-seeking pole.

questions.question: When drawing magnetic field lines, arrows are always included on the lines. What do these arrows show?
options: The direction of the electrical current that created the magnetic field.
The direction in which the north-seeking pole of another magnet would be forced.
The direction in which a south-seeking pole of another magnet would be forced.
The direction of gravity acting on the magnetic material.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key rule when drawing or interpreting magnetic field lines?
options: Magnetic field lines can cross each other if the magnetic field is extremely strong.
Magnetic field lines start at the north pole and stop abruptly in empty space.
Magnetic field lines do not cross over each other and are continuous.
Field lines always run parallel to each other and can never be curved.

questions.question: An electromagnetic door lock on a secure gate is designed to keep the gate locked when there is an active electrical current. How does this mechanism work?
options: The current heats up the lock, causing the metal to expand and jam the gate shut.
The active electromagnet attracts a magnetic bolt, holding it in a position that keeps the gate locked.
The current creates a static charge that repels anyone who tries to touch the gate handle.
The electromagnet generates a magnetic field that physically repels the gate away from the frame.

questions.question: In an electric bell, what is the immediate role of the electromagnet when the switch is pressed?
options: It heats up a bimetallic strip, which bends to strike the bell.
It attracts a striker arm, moving it so that it hits the bell.
It repels the bell itself, causing the bell to vibrate and make a sound.
It generates a radio wave that activates a digital speaker inside the bell.

questions.question: How does an electric bell achieve a continuous ringing sound rather than just a single strike when the switch is held down?
options: The electromagnet is connected to an alternating current that naturally turns on and off 50 times a second.
As the electromagnet moves the striker to hit the bell, it breaks its own circuit, letting the striker spring back to remake the circuit.
The bell has a thermal switch that turns off the current when the wire gets hot and turns it back on when it cools down.
The user must rapidly tap the switch button up and down to make the bell ring continuously.

questions.question: A student sets up a straight copper wire connected to a battery. They place four plotting compasses around the wire. When the switch is closed, what will happen to the compass needles?
options: They will all point directly towards the wire.
They will all point directly away from the wire.
They will align in a circular pattern around the wire, showing a magnetic field.
They will remain pointing towards the Earth's magnetic north.

questions.question: An engineer is designing an electromagnetic crane to lift scrap metal. To increase the maximum lifting capacity without changing the battery or current, which modification should they make?
options: Increase the number of turns of wire in the coil.
Decrease the number of turns of wire in the coil.
Use a thicker plastic coating on the wire.
Use a non-magnetic core like copper.

questions.question: A student wants to double the strength of an electromagnet's magnetic field. Assuming the circuit components can handle it, what change to the electrical circuit would achieve this?
options: Replace the battery with one that provides twice the current.
Add a resistor in series to decrease the current by half.
Replace the wire with one of higher electrical resistance.
Add another switch in series with the battery.

questions.question: A student winds a coil for an electromagnet using bare copper wire, ensuring the loops are tightly wrapped and touching each other. When they connect it to a power supply, the electromagnet fails to attract paperclips. Why does this happen?
options: The current flows directly across the touching loops instead of around the coil.
Bare copper cannot conduct electricity when coiled.
The magnetic field of each loop cancels out the next loop's field.
Copper is a magnetic material and absorbs all the magnetic field.

questions.question: Why does inserting a soft iron rod into the center of a current-carrying coil dramatically increase the strength of the resulting electromagnet?
options: The iron core becomes magnetised when the current is turned on, adding to the field.
The iron core increases the electrical current flowing through the copper wire.
The iron core is a permanent magnet that remains magnetised forever.
The iron core acts as an insulator, stopping magnetic field lines from escaping.

questions.question: How does coiling a long wire multiple times affect the magnetic field compared to a single straight wire carrying the same current?
options: The magnetic fields of individual loops cancel each other out, making the total field weaker.
The magnetic fields of the loops add together, creating a much stronger combined field.
The coiling converts the magnetic field from a circular shape to a straight-line shape only.
The magnetic field remains exactly the same strength but changes direction.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a key advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent bar magnet in industrial sorting of ferrous scrap metal?
options: An electromagnet can be switched on to pick up metal and switched off to drop it.
An electromagnet does not require any source of energy to maintain its magnetic field.
An electromagnet only attracts non-magnetic metals like aluminium and copper.
An electromagnet's magnetic poles cannot be reversed like a permanent magnet's.

questions.question: Two unmarked bar magnets are suspended by threads close to each other. If end A of the first magnet moves away from end B of the second magnet, what can be concluded about these two ends?
options: End A and End B have the same magnetic polarity.
End A and End B have opposite magnetic polarities.
One of the bars is made of a non-magnetic material.
Both ends must be north-seeking poles.

questions.question: An iron nail is placed near a strong bar magnet. What happens to the nail when it is placed near the north-seeking pole compared to when it is placed near the south-seeking pole?
options: It is attracted to the north-seeking pole and repelled by the south-seeking pole.
It is repelled by the north-seeking pole and attracted to the south-seeking pole.
It is attracted to both the north-seeking pole and the south-seeking pole.
It is repelled by both the north-seeking pole and the south-seeking pole.

questions.question: A student is testing various metal rods to see if they are attracted to a magnet. Which group of rods will all be attracted to the magnet?
options: Iron, cobalt, and nickel rods
Copper, aluminum, and gold rods
Iron, brass, and silver rods
Zinc, lead, and tin rods

questions.question: Why does a freely suspended bar magnet always align itself so that its north-seeking pole points towards the Earth's geographic North Pole?
options: The Earth behaves as if it has a giant magnetic field that exerts forces on the magnet.
The Earth's gravity pulls the heavier north-seeking pole of the magnet downward.
The North Pole contains large surface deposits of pure permanent magnets.
Air currents in the atmosphere flow from north to south, pushing the magnet.

questions.question: How does a plotting compass help map the magnetic field around a bar magnet?
options: The compass needle lines up with the magnetic field lines at each point.
The compass needle points directly to the center of the magnet at all times.
The compass needle spins continuously when placed in a magnetic field.
The compass measures the strength of the magnetic field by changing color.

questions.question: If you trace a magnetic field line outside a bar magnet, what is its path from start to end?
options: It can be followed from the north-seeking pole to the south-seeking pole.
It starts at the south-seeking pole and ends at the north-seeking pole.
It starts at the center of the magnet and radiates outwards in all directions.
It loops around the equator of the magnet without touching either pole.

questions.question: When drawing magnetic field lines, what do the arrows printed on the lines represent?
options: The direction of the force that a north-seeking pole of another magnet would experience.
The direction of the electrical current flowing inside the magnet.
The speed at which magnetic radiation travels through space.
The direction that a south-seeking pole would be pushed.

questions.question: Which of the following is a fundamental rule when drawing magnetic field lines to represent a magnetic field?
options: The lines can cross each other where the magnetic field is strongest.
The lines are continuous and never cross over each other.
The lines always start and end at the exact same pole.
The lines stop existing once they are more than 10 centimeters away from the magnet.

questions.question: How does an electromagnetic door lock use electric current to unlock a door?
options: The electromagnet is powered to pull a magnetic bolt to unlock the door.
The electromagnet is powered to push a non-magnetic bolt into the door frame.
The electric current heats up a wax cylinder to melt the lock's bolt.
A permanent magnet is demagnetised permanently by the electric current.

questions.question: In a traditional electric bell, what is the direct role of the electromagnet when the switch is first pressed?
options: It attracts and moves the striker, making it hit the bell.
It heats up a bimetallic strip to push the striker against the bell.
It repels the bell itself, causing the bell to slide towards the striker.
It generates a high-voltage spark that makes a ringing sound.

questions.question: Why does an electric bell ring repeatedly in a rapid 'clapper' motion rather than just hitting the bell once and staying there?
options: As the electromagnet moves the striker, it breaks its own circuit, letting the striker spring back.
The battery automatically switches its polarity back and forth fifty times per second.
The magnetic field of the electromagnet naturally pulsates because of the metal of the bell.
The striker is made of a permanent magnet that is repelled as soon as it touches the bell.

questions.question: Inside a simple electric motor, what causes the central coil of wire to keep spinning?
options: When there is a current in the spinning coil, other magnets around it push it round.
The electric current physically blows air against the rotor, forcing it to spin like a windmill.
The wire is heated by the current, causing it to expand and contract rapidly to create rotation.
Gravitational forces act on the electric charge in the coil to pull it downward.

questions.question: A student makes two electromagnets using identical iron cores, identical wire, and the same current. Electromagnet A has its 50 turns of wire wrapped tightly together in a short 2 cm section. Electromagnet B has its 50 turns spaced out widely over a 10 cm section. Which electromagnet is stronger, and why?
options: Electromagnet A, because more closely spaced coils of wire produce a stronger magnetic field.
Electromagnet B, because spreading the coils over a larger area concentrates the magnetic field lines.
Both are equally strong because they have the same number of turns and the same current.
Electromagnet B, because the wider spacing allows more air to cool the wires and reduce resistance.

questions.question: A student has four solid metal rods: one made of copper, one of nickel, one of zinc, and one of aluminium. She brings a bar magnet near each rod. Which rod will experience an attractive force from both the north and south poles of the magnet?
options: The copper rod
The nickel rod
The zinc rod
The aluminium rod

questions.question: A suspension system uses an unmarked metal block and a permanent bar magnet. When the North pole of the magnet is brought near the block, it attracts. When the magnet is flipped so the South pole is near the block, what will happen?
options: The block will be repelled by the South pole
The block will be attracted by the South pole
The block will experience no force at all
The block will begin to spin continuously

questions.question: Two unmarked bar magnets are placed end-to-end. If they push away from each other with a strong force, what can be concluded about the two touching ends?
options: One end is a North pole and the other is a South pole
Both ends must be North poles
Both ends must be South poles
Both ends are the same type of pole, either both North or both South

questions.question: A student winds a coil of bare copper wire tightly around an iron nail so that the adjacent turns of wire are in direct contact with each other. When they connect the ends of the wire to a battery, the electromagnet does not attract paperclips. What is the most likely reason for this failure?
options: The current bypasses the helical path because the touching bare wires short-circuit across the turns
Bare copper wire is a magnetic material and blocks the magnetic field
Copper cannot carry enough current to create a magnetic field
The iron nail prevents the electrical current from flowing through the wire

questions.question: Why is a soft iron core used in a scrap yard electromagnet rather than a hard steel core?
options: Soft iron is lighter than steel, making the crane easier to maneuver
Soft iron magnetises easily when the current is on and loses its magnetism quickly when the current is turned off
Steel blocks the magnetic field lines, preventing them from reaching the scrap metal
Soft iron acts as an electrical insulator, keeping the current inside the coil

questions.question: A straight copper wire is suspended vertically. When a large direct current is switched on flowing upwards through the wire, what happens to the region immediately surrounding the wire?
options: A static electric charge builds up on the surface of the wire
A circular magnetic field is generated in the space around the wire
The wire becomes permanently magnetised and remains so after the current is off
A magnetic field is generated that points directly upwards, parallel to the wire

questions.question: Why does winding a wire into a circular coil produce a much stronger magnetic field than keeping the same wire straight, assuming the same current flows through it?
options: The coil shape increases the total electrical resistance, which concentrates the energy
The magnetic field around each loop of the coil adds together to create a stronger combined field
Coiling the wire changes the atomic structure of the copper to make it magnetic
The straight wire cancels out its own magnetic field due to gravity

questions.question: Which of the following describes the key functional advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet in industrial sorting systems?
options: Electromagnets always have a stronger magnetic field than any permanent magnet
Electromagnets do not have a South-seeking pole, only a North-seeking pole
The magnetic field of an electromagnet can be switched on to pick up objects and switched off to release them
Electromagnets do not require any materials other than copper wire to function

questions.question: If you suspend a bar magnet horizontally from a lightweight string so that it can rotate freely, why does its north-seeking pole consistently point towards the geographic North Pole of the Earth?
options: The Earth's geographic North Pole contains a massive deposit of pure copper
The Earth has its own magnetic field, and the magnet aligns itself with this field
The rotation of the Earth creates a centrifugal force that pulls only on the north-seeking pole
The Sun's magnetic field pulls the north-seeking pole of all magnets northward

questions.question: When placing several small plotting compasses around a bar magnet, what determines the direction in which each compass needle points?
options: The needles always point towards the geographic North Pole, ignoring the bar magnet
The needles line up with the local magnetic field lines produced by the bar magnet
The needles point directly towards the center of the bar magnet
The needles point perpendicular to the magnetic field lines

questions.question: If you were to trace a magnetic field line outside a bar magnet using a plotting compass, in which direction would your path travel from start to end?
options: From the south-seeking pole to the north-seeking pole
From the center of the magnet outwards in a straight, infinite line
From the north-seeking pole to the south-seeking pole
In a circle that never touches either pole of the magnet

questions.question: What do the arrows drawn on magnetic field lines represent?
options: The direction of the electric current that created the magnetic field
The direction of the force that would act on a north-seeking pole placed at that point
The direction of the force that would act on a south-seeking pole placed at that point
The path that a neutral copper coin would take if released in the field

questions.question: When drawing magnetic field lines around a pair of interacting magnets, which of the following is a fundamental rule that must be followed?
options: Field lines must cross each other at the point of strongest attraction
Field lines must start at the North pole of one magnet and end at the North pole of the other
Field lines must not cross over each other and must be continuous loops
Field lines must always be perfectly straight lines parallel to each other

questions.question: In an electromagnetic door lock system, the door remains securely locked when the power is on. What happens when an authorised user enters a code to unlock the door?
options: The electric current is reversed, which repels the magnetic bolt out of the frame
The electric current is switched off, demagnetising the electromagnet so the magnetic bolt can be released
The current is increased to melt the magnetic lock temporarily
The electromagnet rotates 180 degrees to physically push the door open

questions.question: In a traditional electric bell, why does the striker not just hold tightly against the bell once the electromagnet is turned on?
options: The striker is made of plastic and is not attracted to the magnet for long
The movement of the striker physically breaks the circuit, turning off the electromagnet so the striker can spring back
The battery runs out of charge instantly every time the striker hits the bell
The electromagnet automatically reverses its magnetic poles every millisecond

questions.question: How do the permanent magnets in a simple direct-current motor cause the internal electromagnet (the spinning coil) to rotate?
options: The permanent magnets physically attract the copper wire of the coil because copper is magnetic
The permanent magnets exert forces on the magnetic field produced by the current in the spinning coil, pushing it round
The permanent magnets transfer electric charge to the spinning coil through the air
The permanent magnets block the Earth's magnetic field, allowing the coil to spin freely

questions.question: A student compares two electromagnets. Both have an identical iron core and carry a current of 2 Amps. Electromagnet A has 50 turns of wire, and Electromagnet B has 150 turns of wire. What is the expected difference between them?
options: Electromagnet A will have a stronger magnetic field because fewer turns mean less electrical resistance
Electromagnet B will have a stronger magnetic field because the magnetic fields of more turns of wire add together
Both electromagnets will have the same magnetic field strength because the current is the same
Electromagnet B will not work at all because 150 turns is too many for a 2 Amp current

questions.question: An engineer wants to double the lifting capacity of an industrial electromagnet without changing its physical design or the number of turns in its coil. What modification should they make?
options: Increase the electric current flowing through the coil
Decrease the electric current flowing through the coil
Replace the copper wire with a non-conductive plastic wire
Wrap the entire coil in a thick layer of rubber insulation

questions.question: Two electromagnets, X and Y, are made with the same length of wire and the same iron core. Electromagnet X has its 100 turns wound closely together over a length of 2 cm. Electromagnet Y has its 100 turns spread out loosely over a length of 10 cm. If the same current is passed through both, how will their magnetic fields compare?
options: Electromagnet Y will be stronger because the magnetic field is spread over a larger area
Electromagnet X will be stronger because the closely spaced turns concentrate the magnetic field
They will have identical magnetic field strengths because the number of turns and current are equal
Neither electromagnet will produce a magnetic field because the cores are identical

questions.question: If you map the magnetic field strength at equal distances from the center of a bar magnet, what pattern do you observe regarding its distribution?
options: The magnetic field is significantly stronger on the North side than on the South side
The magnetic field is completely asymmetrical, with random high-strength spots
The magnetic field is symmetrical, showing identical field patterns and strengths on opposite sides of the magnet's axes
The magnetic field only exists on the ends of the magnet and is completely zero along the sides

questions.question: A student has two electromagnets, A and B. Both have identical iron cores and the same current of 1.5 A flowing through them. Electromagnet A has a coil with 50 turns of wire, while Electromagnet B has a coil with 150 turns of wire. How will the magnetic fields of these two electromagnets compare?
options: Electromagnet B's magnetic field will be weaker because the extra wire increases electrical resistance.
Electromagnet A's magnetic field will be three times stronger than Electromagnet B's.
Electromagnet B's magnetic field will be about three times stronger than Electromagnet A's.
Both electromagnets will have the exact same magnetic field strength because the current is the same.

questions.question: An engineer wants to double the strength of an electromagnet's magnetic field without altering the physical design of the coil or core. Which of the following modifications should they make to the circuit?
options: Swap the copper wire of the coil for a wire of identical thickness made of plastic.
Replace the power supply with one that delivers double the electric current.
Add an extra resistor in series to decrease the current by half.
Reverse the direction of the current flowing through the coil.

questions.question: Two electromagnets are made using identical 10 cm iron nails and 2 meters of insulated copper wire. For Electromagnet X, the wire is wound tightly with the coils touching each other along a 2 cm section. For Electromagnet Y, the wire is wound loosely with spaces between the coils along the entire 10 cm length. If the same current is passed through both, which statement is true?
options: Electromagnet X will have a stronger magnetic field because its coils are more closely spaced.
Electromagnet Y will have a stronger magnetic field because the coils cover a greater length of the nail.
Both electromagnets will have identical magnetic field strengths because they use the same length of wire.
Electromagnet X will have no magnetic field because the coils are too close together and cancel each other out.

questions.question: A student winds bare, uninsulated copper wire tightly around an iron nail so that the adjacent turns are touching. When they connect the ends of the wire to a battery, they find that the nail does not become a magnet. Why does this electromagnet fail to work?
options: Bare copper wire is a non-magnetic metal and cannot generate a magnetic field under any circumstances.
The bare wire causes a short circuit that prevents any electric current from leaving the battery.
The touch of adjacent bare wires permanently demagnetises the iron nail core.
The current flows straight across the touching turns along the nail's length rather than flowing around it in a coil.

questions.question: Why does inserting a soft iron rod into the center of a current-carrying coil of wire significantly increase the strength of the magnetic field?
options: The iron core acts as a conductor that allows electric current to flow directly through the center of the coil.
The iron core becomes temporarily magnetised by the coil's field, adding its own strong magnetic field.
The iron core reduces the electrical resistance of the wire coil, allowing a much higher current to flow.
The iron core permanently retains its magnetism, ensuring the electromagnet stays on even when the current is switched off.

questions.question: A straight copper wire is suspended vertically. When a heavy direct current is switched on so that electricity flows upwards through the wire, what happens in the space immediately surrounding the wire?
options: A circular magnetic field is generated around the wire.
The air around the wire becomes permanently magnetised.
A magnetic field is created that points straight up parallel to the wire.
No magnetic field is generated because copper is a non-magnetic metal.

questions.question: If a single loop of current-carrying wire produces a weak magnetic field, how does winding the wire into a multi-loop coil affect the overall magnetic field?
options: The magnetic fields of adjacent loops oppose and cancel each other out, leaving only the outer loops active.
The loops concentrate the electric charge, which increases the voltage but does not change the magnetic field.
The magnetic fields from each individual loop add together to produce a much stronger combined field.
The magnetic field becomes weaker because the current must travel a longer distance through the wire.

questions.question: In a scrap metal yard, an operator uses a crane with a large magnet to pick up old steel car parts, move them, and then drop them into a crusher. Why is an electromagnet used for this task instead of a strong permanent magnet?
options: Permanent magnets only attract iron, whereas electromagnets can attract any metal, including aluminium and copper.
Electromagnets are much lighter than permanent magnets of the same lifting capacity.
An electromagnet does not require any metal components to generate a magnetic field.
An electromagnet can have its magnetism easily turned off by stopping the electric current, allowing the metal parts to fall.

questions.question: A scientist breaks a bar magnet exactly in half down the middle. What is the magnetic state of the two resulting pieces?
options: Each piece becomes a complete magnet with its own north-seeking pole and south-seeking pole.
One piece becomes a pure north-seeking pole and the other piece becomes a pure south-seeking pole.
Both pieces lose their magnetic properties entirely and become non-magnetic.
The pieces will now only attract magnetic materials but will no longer have any poles.

questions.question: Two bar magnets are suspended by threads near each other. If the north-seeking pole of the first magnet is brought close to the north-seeking pole of the second magnet, how will they interact?
options: They will pull towards each other because similar magnetic poles attract.
They will push away from each other because similar magnetic poles repel.
They will not interact because only a north-seeking pole and a south-seeking pole can exert forces.
They will rotate until both north-seeking poles point towards the center of the Earth.

questions.question: An unmagnetised iron nail is placed near a bar magnet. What happens to the nail when it is brought close to the north-seeking pole, and then the south-seeking pole of the magnet?
options: The nail is attracted to the north-seeking pole but is repelled by the south-seeking pole.
The nail is repelled by both the north-seeking pole and the south-seeking pole.
The nail is attracted to both the north-seeking pole and the south-seeking pole.
The nail is attracted to the south-seeking pole but is repelled by the north-seeking pole.

questions.question: A recycling plant wants to separate mixed metals using a powerful conveyor belt magnet. Which group of metal objects will all be attracted to the magnet?
options: A copper wire, an aluminium can, and a gold ring.
An iron bolt, a nickel coin, and a cobalt rod.
